The prevalence figures individually have support, but the 25–35% panel composition claim is a synthesized inference from national prevalence applied to a private GP panel — a material analytical step without direct primary support. Single verifiable primary source for the Malaysia component, none for the Indonesia panel-composition inference. Low.

All secondary = Low. Additionally the 1,500 lab-result-batches/month volume figure is an assumed extrapolation not cited to any source.

Also: the 200 results/month volume is assumed.

claims_scored.claim: Indonesia BPJS Kesehatan spends >IDR 30.5 trillion ($1.88B) annually on DM and HT management

Note: if the Frontiers corroboration from PP2.2(3b) is treated as cross-validating, the score could rise to Medium — however the two citations are in different pain point sections and the Frontiers study does not appear to directly cite the IDR 30.5T figure; it covers FKTP utilization rates. Scored Low here.

claims_scored.claim: December 2023: only 32% of 273 assessed FKTPs met the Level 4 RPPT target

However the rubric is strict: 1 source regardless of category = Low. Identical claim also cited in PP2.2(5) with same URL; cross-referencing within same document does not count as a second independent source.

claims_scored.claim: PDF is the de facto delivery format for GP clinic–lab result handoffs in Indonesia and Malaysia; no primary care standard mandates structured electronic delivery to standalone GP clinics

PMC12036547 (JMIR 2025) documents FHIR interoperability challenges at FKTP level that confirm structured delivery is absent. Meets 2+ sources with ≥1 primary category = Medium. No geography mismatch (both cover Indonesia FHIR/HIE context). The claim is about absence of a standard rather than a measured frequency; both sources corroborate the structural gap.

claims_scored.claim: SATUSEHAT FHIR R4 mandate exists; implementation blocked by: 'FHIR profile selection,' 'mapping EMR data,' 'limited IT staff,' 'absence of customized integration protocols' at FKTP level
sources: PP2.1(9) researchgate.net — SATUSEHAT interoperability evaluation literature review [secondary-trade/preprint]

PMC12036547 (JMIR 2025) is a peer-reviewed primary academic source directly studying SATUSEHAT developer community pain points — the quoted pain-point phrases likely derive from this paper. ResearchGate source (9) is a literature review / preprint — secondary category. 2 sources with ≥1 primary = Medium. Covers Indonesia specifically.

claims_scored.claim: Malaysia myHIX progresses in MOH hospitals but private GP clinic connectivity is not a documented near-term rollout target

claims_scored.claim: In a Malaysian public primary care 10-clinic study, only 2 of 10 clinics had complete on-site HbA1c testing; 8 depended on external lab referrals via paper/manual processes
claims_scored.rationale: Single primary-academic source. 1 source = Low regardless of quality. Additionally: this is a public primary care study (Klinik Kesihatan), not private GP clinics — a public-to-private proxy acknowledged in the draft.

claims_scored.claim: Unstructured data constitutes ~80% of healthcare data; OCR + LLM can extract structured fields from lab report PDFs

claims_scored.claim: Of 7.4 million JKN-diagnosed DM patients, only 2.8 million (37.8%) regularly access FKTP; of 20.5 million JKN-diagnosed HT patients, only 5.6 million (27.3%) actively visit FKTP

The Frontiers study (3b) directly addresses FKTP utilization rates for CDM, providing the primary-academic corroboration needed. Despite (3a) being inaccessible, (3b) independently confirms the utilization gap concept even if the specific 37.8%/27.3% figures trace to BPJS administrative data via Kompas. 2 sources with ≥1 primary-academic = Medium. Note: the exact BPJS figures (37.8%, 27.3%) may trace to the same BPJS administrative dataset cited differently — chain-of-citations risk. Scored Medium, flagged.

claims_scored.claim: Nurse labor for manual recall: ~1.5–3 hours/week at 300-patient-panel clinic; IDR 5M/month ($309/month) Indonesia; MYR 2,249/month ($484/month) Malaysia — equals $10–$22/week (ID) or $16–$34/week (MY) in direct recall labor

Salary data from aggregators is secondary-only with no primary labor statistics source. No BPS Indonesia or DOSM Malaysia primary data. Compounded proxy (assumed time × aggregator salary) = Low.

claims_scored.claim: PROLANIS performance bonus at risk: FKTP with 1,000 enrolled BPJS participants at IDR 12,000/month capitation earns IDR 12M/month base; performance adjustment 5–15%; missing RPPT loses IDR 600,000–1,800,000/month (~$37–$111/month)

claims_scored.claim: Malaysia NHMS 2023: DM prevalence 15.6% (of which 9.7% known); hypertension 29.2% (of which 17.3% known)

NHMS 2023 MOH Malaysia — underlying primary-ministry source cited indirectly

weak_claims_to_deep_research.claim_text: Staff time for manual lab result transcription or filing: ~3–4 hours/week at a multi-provider clinic handling ~1,500 batches/month; manual transcription generates 3–5% error rate on numeric fields at ~$45–65/incident rework cost
current_sources: rovinghealth.com healthcare administrative burden blog [secondary-trade, sole source for both the time benchmark and the error rate]
weak_claims_to_deep_research.issue: Both the labor time benchmark (3–4 hrs/week) and the transcription error rate (3–5%) with rework cost ($45–65/incident) trace entirely to a single industry blog (rovinghealth.com). This is the foundational cost anchor for PP2.1 — the entire $55–95/month and $270–$650/month cost estimates rest on it. No time-motion study, no peer-reviewed study of lab result transcription error rates, and no ID/MY-specific data.
weak_claims_to_deep_research.suggested_action: Search for peer-reviewed studies on manual clinical data transcription error rates, preferably in primary care or lab result contexts. Specific queries: (1) 'manual transcription error rate laboratory results primary care' in PubMed/PMC; (2) 'healthcare data entry error rate numeric fields' in JMIR or BMC journals; (3) search for any Malaysian or Indonesian study on EHR data entry accuracy. Also search: 'administrative burden lab result management primary care time-motion study' for time benchmarks.

weak_claims_to_deep_research.claim_text: Only 32% of 273 assessed FKTPs met the Level 4 RPPT target (controlled CDM ratio) as of December 2023
weak_claims_to_deep_research.issue: This is the single most important quantified claim in Stage 2 — it anchors the scale of CDM recall failure across all PP2.2 cost calculations and the gate case for the entire CDM operations opportunity. The source (BPJS Kesehatan Journal) is high-quality and directly authoritative, but it is a single source. One corroborating citation from a different outlet (Kemenkes annual report, a peer-reviewed analysis of PROLANIS performance, or a Frontiers/Lancet paper citing this figure) would immediately upgrade this to High and solidify the foundation of the entire PP2.2 argument.
weak_claims_to_deep_research.suggested_action: Search for corroboration of the 32% FKTP RPPT Level 4 achievement figure from: (1) Kemenkes Profil Kesehatan Indonesia 2023 or 2024 — check whether RPPT performance statistics are reported; (2) search PMC/PubMed for 'PROLANIS RPPT performance Indonesia 2023' or 'BPJS capitation performance-based Indonesia'; (3) search Google Scholar for 'Hasil Pemantauan Pelaksanaan Program Pengelolaan Penyakit Kronis' to find official Kemenkes monitoring reports.

weak_claims_to_deep_research.claim_text: GP clinics in Malaysia and Indonesia experience no-show rates of 15–30% for booked appointments
current_sources: PMC10624443 HKL 2019 outpatient study (Malaysia, hospital context) [primary-academic, single source]
PMC11436967 Malaysia tertiary dietetic clinic 2017 [primary-academic, single source, specialist context]
PMC4714455 global review [primary-academic, global, single source]
weak_claims_to_deep_research.current_score: Low (per individual sub-claims); no verified Indonesia GP clinic figure exists
weak_claims_to_deep_research.issue: The 15–30% claim is the foundational frequency for PP2.3 (no-show) and drives all revenue-loss and slot-waste calculations. The Malaysia evidence is from hospital outpatient (HKL) and a specialist dietetic clinic — neither is a private GP clinic. No Indonesia GP clinic no-show rate is cited at all (acknowledged in the text as 'No verified Indonesia GP clinic no-show rate found'). A GP-clinic-specific no-show study for either market would be transformative for this section.
weak_claims_to_deep_research.suggested_action: Search for: (1) Malaysian GP clinic no-show rates specifically — 'appointment no-show general practitioner Malaysia private clinic' in PubMed/PMC/Google Scholar; (2) BookDoc or Klinify published analytics on GP booking completion rates (may be in tech press or company blog, but even secondary confirmation helps directionally); (3) any Indonesian study on appointment no-show or patient non-attendance at klinik pratama — search 'tidak hadir janji temu klinik pratama Indonesia'; (4) check if Malaysia MOH Primary Care Division has published statistics on appointment utilization in Klinik Kesihatan (public, but provides directional baseline).

notable_source_improvements_vs_stage_1: Multiple peer-reviewed PROLANIS studies (PMC12538241, PMC10576047, PMC11422728) are directly on-topic for Indonesia CDM recall — stronger domain fit than Stage 1's US/proxy reliance
Malaysia NHMS 2023 and NDR 2023 data cited (via Scientific Reports and MOH publication) — primary-ministry tier for Malaysia CDM prevalence
BPJS Kesehatan Journal (primary-ministry) cited for RPPT performance — authoritative for Indonesia CDM programme outcomes
JMIR Formative Research 2025 and Frontiers in Health Services 2025 both directly on-topic for Indonesia FHIR/CDM context
Two RCTs for reminder efficacy (PMC9126539, PMC5130951) provide strong causal evidence for PP2.3 intervention validity
persistent_gaps_vs_stage_1: All cost anchors (labor time for transcription, recall dispatch, no-show handling) remain either assumed or sourced from a single secondary-trade blog (rovinghealth.com) — no time-motion study for ID/MY private GP context
Salary data still from JobStreet/Indeed aggregators — no BPS Indonesia or DOSM Malaysia primary labor statistics
No Indonesia GP clinic-level no-show rate found; hospital proxy used
Malaysia myHIX status claim uses a 2021 article — needs current policy source
gate_reasoning: Of 37 claims scored, 3 are High confidence (PROLANIS recall failure composite from 3 independent primary-academic sources; BPJS FKTP CDM utilization gap with Frontiers + BPJS Journal corroboration; reminder-efficacy RCT evidence). 9 claims reach Medium, primarily where 2 independent primary-academic sources converge on the same finding (SATUSEHAT FHIR barriers, NHMS 2023 prevalence, Malaysia HbA1c control rates, FHIR PDF-delivery gap). 25 claims are Low — driven by single-source citations for high-quality BPJS/Kemenkes data (which need one corroborating independent source to upgrade), assumed labor time and fee benchmarks, and secondary-trade sources for operating cost estimates. The central strength of Stage 2 versus Stage 1 is that the core epidemiological and programme-performance claims now have primary-tier sources (BPJS Kesehatan Journal, NHMS 2023, peer-reviewed PROLANIS studies) that directly cover the target geography. The core weakness is that the cost model for PP2.1 (lab result parsing labor) rests entirely on a single industry blog for its two key parameters (time benchmark and error rate), and cost models for PP2.2 and PP2.3 continue to compound assumed-frequency inputs with secondary-trade salary data. Three weak claims are flagged for deep research, prioritized: (1) lab result transcription error rate and labor benchmark — needs a peer-reviewed source to replace the single blog citation; (2) RPPT 32% figure corroboration — one additional citation would upgrade the strongest pain-point anchor from Low to High; (3) GP-clinic-specific no-show rate for Malaysia/Indonesia — hospital proxies currently carry the entire PP2.3 frequency case.
